matched_finding.description: Contradictory experimental design description: The manuscript describes the experimental setup as a "single within-subject design," but the statistical reporting contradicts this. The degrees of freedom for the residuals in the ANOVA (df = 994) and the mutually exclusive sample sizes per condition in Table 7 (which sum to the total N = 1000) indicate a between-subjects design. Please clarify the experimental design and ensure that the terminology and statistical models applied correctly align with how participants were actually exposed to the conditions.

matched_finding.description: Self-selection invalidates random assignment: The authors state that participants selected their own conditions. Allowing participants to self-select into experimental groups eliminates random assignment, introducing severe selection bias and confounding variables. This fundamentally undermines the ability to make causal inferences about the identifiable victim effect or the intervention, and it represents a major departure from the original experimental design. If this is a typographical error and participants were indeed randomly assigned, please correct the text. If self-selection was actually used, the statistical analyses must be completely overhauled to account for observational data, and all causal claims must be downgraded.
matched_finding.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

matched_finding.description: Contradictory hypothesis and conclusion: There is a direct contradiction between the stated hypothesis and the conclusion drawn in the abstract. In the introduction, the authors hypothesize that people will perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim. However, the abstract claims that the results supported the hypothesis by showing a lower rating of perceived impact for the identifiable victim. The authors must ensure that the theoretical predictions and the interpretation of the findings are logically consistent.
matched_finding.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.
